text: Johnson's next observation follows from the last, and he put it in a sentence that has been quoted ever since: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He meant it as praise. The tragic writers of his own century had filled their stages with princes who spoke in exalted periods and acted from motives no spectator had ever felt; their virtue was too perfect and their villainy too complete to be recognised. Shakespeare's persons, by Johnson's account, speak as the reader himself would have spoken had he stood where they stand. Their grief is ordinary grief, and their anger has the shape anger takes in common life. This holds even where the action leaves common life behind. A ghost may walk on the battlements, or witches may meet upon a heath, and still the talk of the men who see them stays level with what any reader knows of fear and doubt. The marvel belongs to the story, while the speech remains human. Johnson thought that this kept the plays credible when their events were least so, and he counted it among Shakespeare's chief excellences.
